The structural characterization of DELs has been considered one of the most authentic ways to confirm the formation of a particular DEL system and the majority of researchers have followed variations in physiochemical parameters to confirm the formation of DELs. Some researchers [25,26] have applied differential scanning colorimetry (DSC) while many others used simple cryoscope. [27] In DSC, 10-20 mg of liquids have been taken in aluminum pans and cooled to various temperatures followed by heating at a particular ramp rate to monitor various thermal transitions. The pres- ence of endotherms at different temperature and their com- parison with the DSC thermogram of parent HBD and HBA species can help us to establish the eutectic point of DEL and the presence of heterogeneity (if any). Besides, theoret- ical models like molecular dynamics (MD) and radial distri- bution function (RDF) have successfully predicted the number of hydrogen bonds and linkage between vari- ous atoms. [26] Likewise, the presence of hydrogen bonds formed due to HBD and HBA are of special character and can be easily detected by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR). For this purpose, the NMR spectra of HBD, HBD, and DEL are often compared. For example, the DEL system comprising ChCl:n-butyric acid when dissolved in DMSO-d₆ exhibited an additional peak at 6.93 ppm that indicates the appearance of intermolecular hydrogen bonds. [28] The infrared spectroscopy under Fourier-Transformation mode (FT-IR) stands among the most convenient and frequently applied techniques for DEL characterization. For every DEL system the appearance, disappearance, and broadening of peaks in the range between 1500 and 4000 cm⁻¹ establish the formation of the resultant DEL. For example, the OH signal of propylene glycol becomes broader due to the formation of hydrogen bonds. [29] Unlike, the disappearance of signal of the methyl group (3025 cm⁻¹) of ChCl indicates the interaction of this methyl group and another. Recently, Cui and Kuroda [26] applied two dimensional infrared (2DIR) to probe into the variation in molecular environment and entanglement between the location and orientation of vari- ous groups. The 2DIR can directly monitor the difference in molecular arrangements of HBDs and HBAs. ## Phase behavior The key features of any DEL system depend on the eutectic composition and nature of hydrogen bond donors and acceptors. There exist two logics regarding deep depression at the freezing point (beyond a eutectic point). The first considers the eutectic point as a colligative effect and the second says crystallization may seize due to intercalation of HBDs into HBAs, and the resulting combination has the lowest possible melting point. The phase diagram in Figure 3 depicts the depression in the melting temperature of B due to the Intercalation of A and vice versa. In the case of deep eutectic liquids (DELs), an unexpected deep depression of the freezing point takes place for the simultaneous development of different interactions between HBA and HBD. According to Zhekenov et al., [15] in the formation of choline chloride (ChCl) containing DELs, where ChCl act as HBA and urea (U), ethylene glycol (EG), and Glycerol (GY) act as HBDs, a decrease in the number of hydrogen bonds and intermolecular interaction between pure components results in the formation of low melting liquids. In particular, the interaction energy of ChCl before and after mixing decreases significantly. Moreover, the number of interactions and their resultant strength in the final low melting liquids vary with HBD. For example, EG and GY may attract anion with −5.0 × 10^4 and −3.5 × 10^4 kJ/mol energies, respectively, whereas, urea has a weak interaction with anion. 1638 M. MUSHTAQ ET AL. The intercalation often occurs when HBD and HBA of compatible size, charge, and nature are mixed in a particular ratio. Therefore, eutectic points can furnish important infor-mation about the composition, temperature range, and physiochemical characteristics of any eutectic system for a particular application. For example, ChCl and glycerol melt at 281, 237, and 241 K when mixed in the stoichiometric ratios of 1:1, 1:2, and 1:3, respectively. [30] Similarly, the physiochemical properties like melting points, surface ten-sion, viscosity, refractive index, and pH change with the change in molar composition. [31] Researchers have also tried to identify the eutectic compositions by changing the com-positions of HBA and HBD. [32] A cite worthy break-through regarding the hydrophobi- city of deep eutectic liquids has been documented by Longeras et al. [33] These researchers prepared the aqueous solution of a deep-eutectic liquid comprising lidocaine and oleic acid (1:1) and observed that a 50/50 mixture of water and deep-eutectic liquid form a single transparent liquid phase at 20°C. The phase separation occurred at 25°C (the lower critical solution temperature of the prepared deep eutectic liquid). It was further noted that an interface between water and the deep eutectic mixture of lidocaine and oleic acid appears once the temperature rises to 25°C and disappears below 24°C. The components of deep eutec- tic liquid can accumulate in the hydrophobic phase and move exclusively toward the aqueous phase. These types of deep eutectic liquids may work more efficiently to extract pollutants, dyes, and other bioactive substances. A mathematical relationship between eutectic compos- ition and enthalpy of transition can be produced by follow- ing Equation 1. Here Xᵢᴸ, ΔHᵢ, and Tmᵢ stand for mole fraction, enthalpy, and the melting point of the pure com- pound. [34] LnXᵢᴸ = - \frac{\Delta H_i}{RT} \left\{1 - \frac{T}{Tm_i}\right\} (1) For many combinations, these systems are also labeled as designer liquids that can be utilized more effectively by studying various other compositions apart from the eutectic one due to their changing dynamics and properties. Besides, the formation of deep-eutectic liquids often follows the first-order kinetics (Equation 1) for the activation parameters. For example, the formation of ChCl:urea, the most famous DEL, is an endothermic process with an enthalpy change of about 30 kJ mol⁻¹. Applying the Arrhenius equation establishes low activation energy (up to 11 kJ mol⁻¹) and a more prominent pre-exponential factor for the ChCl:urea. Likewise, positive entropy of formation and negative Gibbs function indicates the process is reasonably fast. ## Hydrogen bonding The classical deep eutectic liquids (DELs) are low melting mixtures of general formula [NPS]⁺X⁻NY, where NPS are organic cations of ammonium, phosphonium, or sulphonium species carrying transferable Lewis base, i.e., Halide anion, and Y represents Hydrogen bond donors. However, certain studies describe the halogen-free liquids mainly com- prising alkali acetate, triflate, and bistriflimide as HBA and polyalcohols as HBD. [35] The main forces of interaction holding the components of deep eutectic liquids together are hydrogen bonds; however, π- interactions and Van der Waal forces are also notified. Overall, a cascade of hydrogen bonds, i.e., weaker, moderate, and stronger may exist between HBD and HBA species depending upon their inher- ent polarity. The key factor behind the lowering of melting point in any DEL apart from ionic and steric effects is hydrogen bonding. According to Arunan et al., [36] there is a charge transfer between HBA and HBD molecules as a result of which, a partial covalent bond is formed between the two molecules which can be identified via NMR, or FTIR. Pimentel and McClellan [37] highlighted the impact of hydro-gen bonding on various properties like melting point, dens-ity, vapor pressure, and viscosity of DEL systems. The authors also noticed that a change in H-bond interactions is related to the change in density as the increase in density would decrease the free volume. The number of hydroxyl groups at vicinal position often lead to intracts within the molecules of HBDs themselves. For example, Ozturk et al. [38] observed that the glycerol-containing DEL system exhibited higher density due to a higher number (three) of hydroxyl groups available for H-bonding. The DEL system containing ethylene glycol also exhibit higher density at the eutectic point than pure HBD due to the enhancement of H-bonding. In contrast, the glycerol-based DEL system exhibited minimum density at the eutectic point due to dis-ruption of H-bonding. This creates serious interest in the role of H-bonding for a DEL system as both combinations had the same HBA. However, the difference in H-bonding compelled the systems to follow completely different mecha-nisms. [38] Stefanovic et al. reported that a similar H-bond pattern was present in DEL systems based on ChCl, ethylene glycol, and glycerol, while DEL containing ChCl and urea exhibited a unique pattern that differs in hydrogen-bonded networks. [39] Ashworth et al. [40] studied hydrogen bond interaction between components ChCl and urea containing DELs and reported that there happen different type of hydrogen bond interactions (substantial, regular, and weak) between the components, and the bonding is somewhat transient, which means that the molecules can switch their sites whenever they want to. This explains the anomalous behavior of DEL systems regarding glassy behavior and high viscosities. [40] These studies highlight that H-bonding plays a pivotal role in each DEL combination. Tailorable features of deep eutectic liquids A variety of electrostatic interactions no doubt complicate the assessment, but at the same time, it generates an equal number of polarity, viscosities, surface tension, and density arrangements. Figure 3 manifests the tailorable physico-chemical properties of DELs and it would be fair to imagine the hydrogen bonding network of DEL resembles the CRITICAL REVIEWS IN ANALYTICAL CHEMISTRY <::icon: teacup in circle::> 1639 structure of spider's webs where the strength of each thread and their connectivity affects these physicochemi- cal attributes. ## Polarity Polarity plays the most crucial role in deciding the depth of eutectic point (melting temperature, vapor pressure, and other physicochemical parameters associated with DELs), especially for those designed to replace the organic solvents being used in industry and academia. In the case of organic solvent, polarity expresses its ability to solvate various species and facilitate their dissolution or solvation. The polarity of DELs depends upon the cascade of bonding forces (H-bond, van Der Waal's interaction, or π-interaction), however, it is difficult to define and almost impossible to assess absolutely. A set of assumptions and methods has been followed to express the polarity in terms of the solvatochromic potential of the DELs, it should be mentioned here that these paradigms also depend on mass transfer rates. Pandey et al. [41] followed the UV visible and molecular fluorescence to probe into polarity-induced vibronic bands. For example, the absorption band of betaine dye 30 (2,6-diphenyl-4-(2,4,6-tri phenyl pyridinium-1-yl)phenolate) shifts from 810 nm (λmax) in non-polar solvent to 453 nm (λmax) in water (polar solvent) due to a charge transfer reaction between phenolate and pyridinium part. The zwitterionic nature of dye has been frequently exploited as a solvatochromic probe, and the presence of hydrogen bonding donating species stabilizes the ground state of dye. An empirical scale (ET30= 28591.5/λmax) expresses the molar transition energy (kcal mol⁻¹) at standard temperature and pressure. However, owing to the solubility restrictions, other probes have been developed. Almost all photo-inducible charge-transfer probes depend upon the hydrogen bonding ability of DELs and the strength of interaction between HBD and HBA. Wojeicchowski et al. [42] studied the Kamlet-Taft (K-T) parameters associated with the solvatochromic potential of solvents. The K-T model parameters describe the polarizabil- ity (π*), hydrogen bond accepting ability (β), and hydrogen bond denoting ability (α). After calculating the properties, including (a) misfit interaction energy (Emf), (b) van der Waals interaction energy (Evdw), hydrogen bond accept moment (MHBA), and hydrogen bond denote moment (MHBD) for 175 organic solvents, the approach was extended to various types of DELs following Equations 2-4. $\pi^* = X_1 M_{HBA} + X_2 M_{HBD} + X_3 E_{mf} + X_4$ (2) $\beta = X_1 M_{HBA} + X_2 M_{HBD} + X_3 E_{vdW} + X_4$ (3) $\alpha = X_1 M_{HBA} + X_2 M_{HBD} + X_3 E_{vdW} + X_4$ (4) Finally, comparing predicted values of K-T model param- eters for organic solvents and deep eutectic liquids indicates that the latter can have a broader range of polarities. Likewise, Florindo et al. [43] observed that the structure of HBA in a DEL system controls the polarity/polarizability, and K-T model parameters remain almost the same within a particular family of DEL; however, these parameters differ among the various families of DEL, whether they are made up of salts like ChCl, tertiary amines, acids or neutral compounds. Similarly, the substitution of HBD often changes the solvatochromic behavior of the resultant DEL. ## Viscosity The higher viscosities of DELs are a key hurdle in their use for various applications, particularly in extraction technol-ogy. The relative strength and number of hydrogen bonds shift the melting point deep below the eutectic point and the same can increase the viscosity of the resultant liquid. However, the geometry, shape, and size of molecules also contribute to their resistance in flow dynamics. It has been noted that pure DEL offers more resistance to change in shape at a given shear rate. The viscosity decreases with the increase in temperature and moisture level. The effect of temperature on the viscosities of DEL has been extensively studied and found to be testable by Arrhenius (Equation 5) and the (Vogel – Fulcher – Tammann) VFT (Equation 6) model. [44,45] ηArrhenius = Ae^E/RT (5) Here, E represents activation energy, R is the molar gas constant, and A is a pre-factor. $\eta_{VFT} = A' e^{B/(T-T_0)}$ (6) where A' represents the pre-exponential factor that quantifies viscosity, B accounts for activation energy, and T₀ corresponds to the glass transition temperature. Keeping these equations in mind, a wide range of studies have been performed to quantify the effect of various factors like mole fractions of HBD/HBA and water content (%). Aroso et al.[46] analyzed various combinations of ChCl and sugars via rheology. As modeled by the Arrhenius equation, the results displayed that every NaDELs combination showed Newtonian behavior.[46] Basaiahgari et al.[47] conducted the same study on benzyl tripropylammonium-based DELs and found that data obtained by the VFT model (Equation 6) were more reliable.[47] Likewise, Cui et al.[48] evaluated the viscosity measurements of DELs comprising ChCl as HBA and acidic HBDs. It was observed that the viscosities of DELs fit better with the VFT equation than the Arrhenius model.[48] Another group of researchers[49] presented two different empirical models built from VFT and Eyring viscosity models as a function of composition and temperature and reported that the VFT model was better fitted for DELs with high viscosities. In contrast, the Eyring model was accurate for low vis- costy DELs. For example, the viscosity measurements of DEL combination of levulinic acid and ChCl have fitted accurately with both Arrhenius and VFT models. [50] It has been reported viscosity of a particular DEL is affected by water content, [51] temperature, [52] and the molar ratio of components. [53] In the case of liquid-liquid or solid-phase extraction, an increase in viscosity reduces the mass transfer during liquid-liquid extraction and other chromatographic 1640 (Open Access icon) M. [29] Overall, there exists a lack of understanding of the specific origin of viscosity in these liquids and above all, the quantitative effect of DELs viscosity on mass transfer or extraction efficiency needs more systematic investigations. ## Density It has been observed that DELs show higher densities than water (mainly in the range of 1.0–1.5 g cm⁻³). Basaiahgari et al. [54] calculated the densities of many combinations of HBAs and HBDs and found that glycerol-based DELs had higher densities than DELs based on ethylene glycol (Table 1). A look at the physiochemical data (Table 1) indicates that the formation of hydrogen bonds due to the increase in the number of -OH functional groups signifies the increase in density as it decreases the free available volume. [54] For example, keeping the same ratios between HBA (ChCl) and HBD (organic acid), the DEL comprising oxalic acid was denser (1.30 g cm⁻³) than malonic acid (1.25 g cm⁻³). Within the same type of DEL, the highest density of 1.46 g cm⁻³ was exhibited by ChCl:trichloroacetic acid (1:2). [48] It has been seen that the densities of DELs can be adjusted by modifying the molar ratio and overall composition. A plethora of predictive tools have been introduced to anticipate the density of liquids, and many of these models have been successfully applied to estimate the density of DELs. Rackett [55] was the first to modify the equation of state to calculate the molar volume and density (Equation 7) of saturated liquids. However, the model can successfully predict the densities of DELs. ρ = M⁻¹ { (RT_c / P_c) (P_c v_c / T_c)^(1 + (1 - T/T_c)^0.2857) } (7) Later on, several amendments in Equation 7 were suggested by Spencer and Danner, [56] Mjalli et al., [57] and Haghbakhsh et al. [58] The density of DELs in these models was declared to be the function of the critical state variable (P_c, T_c, and V_c) and acentric factor (ω). A detailed study[59] was conducted by varying citric acid and choline chloride molar ratios. It was observed that an increase in the amount of HBA (ChCl) in the overall com- bination can decrease the density and vice versa. The den- sities of DELs can be changed by varying temperatures, where an increase in temperature will decrease the densities. A similar kind of trend (a linear relationship between temperature and DEL's density) exists for nine different combinations of DEL systems. [61] Few other researchers have reported a negative linear rela- tionship with DEL systems like ethylene-glycol-based, [62] choline chloride, varying HBDs, [63] and Ni (II) salt. [64] It has been reported that the density of a particular DEL depends mainly on the molar ratio and the nature of the hydrogen bond donor. [48,53,65] ## Surface tension In addition to density and viscosity, the surface tension of a DEL can play an essential role in its use as an extraction solvent. Besides, the knowledge of surface tension can be linked with the nature of interactions in a particular DEL system. Increasing surface tension can reduce the mass transfer phenomenon during separation processes like extraction, distillation, evaporation, absorption, and crystallization. Likewise, with other physicochemical features, these liquids' surface tension can also be predicted using a quantitative structure-property relationship. The most frequently applied model uses the density data in terms of parachor, [66] or molar volume. [55] The more straightforward ways to calculate the surface tension of liquids involve but are not limited to using a pendant drop, [67] Wilhelmy plate, [68] or a Du Noüy ring. [69] For more comprehensive relationships, we need to correlate the changes in the overall environment of the DEL system and its surface tension. Gajardo-Parra et al. evaluated the surface tension of three different combinations of DELs systems made up of ChCl and found that ChCl acted as a surfactant to decrease the cohesive forces resulting in a decrease in the surface of the final DEL combinations as compared to the neat compo- nents. [63] Hayyan et al. tried to explain the role of the ChCl concentration towards the surface tension its DEL systems. Various combinations of DELs were prepared by varying concentrations of ChCl, and results indicate that increase in the molar amount of ChCl increased the surface tension of DEL. [70] It has been also observed that an increase in tem- perature results in a linear decrease in the surface tension of a particular DEL. [71,72] **Vapor pressure** The pressure exerted by the vapors of a substance in equilib-rium with its condensed phase is termed vapor pressure. The knowledge of vapor pressure is equally important for these designer liquids to work as extraction solvents. Besides, the value of vapor pressure can help us to predict the nature of DEL constituents and the extent of interaction present between these constituents. Nevertheless, very few studies on direct or indirect measurement of the vapor pres-sure of deep eutectic liquids (DELs) have been conducted so far. The most frequently adopted instrumental approach for the determination of vapor pressure follows Equation 9 of conventional thermogravimetric analysis, [73] in which dm/dt, M, T, and K denote weight loss rate, molecular mass, tem-perature (K), and constant representing the extent of molecular interaction in a particular DEL system. A study conducted by Su et al.[81] describes the effect of the type and concentration of HBD on the refractive index of DEL keeping HBA same. The results indicate that DEL containing tetrabutylammonium chloride (TBAC) and phenylacetic acid had a greater RI than DEL containing TBAC and propionic acid due to the bulky phenyl group. Similarly, Sánchez et al.[82] evaluated the molar refractivity of seven DEL combinations of L-proline and betaine and found that it depends on HBD molar concentration. In addition to the above-cited features, the pH of a DEL system is a vital factor for defining its characteristics along with other industrial applications. Hayyan et al. [31] tested the pH of various DEL combinations of varying molar compositions of ChCl and glucose. They reported a linear dependence of pH with temperatures from 25 to 85°C and concluded that these mixtures could be used commercially. [31] Skulcova et al. [83] reported a linear decrease of pH as the temperature was increased for seven different combinations of DEL with significant influence created by the type of HBD used. [83] Meanwhile, a few authors like Zhang et al. [84] compared the extraction efficiency of different combinations of DEL by varying pH from 4 to 10 and found that pH had no significant effect on the extraction efficiency of proteins. Due to their high ionic conductivity, DEL finds potential uses in power systems like advanced electrolytes for batteries. [85–87] It has been reported that the ionic conductivity of these solvents is lower than salts in molten states. According to hole theory, Abbott et al. explained this differ- ence based on ionic size and viscosity. [88] In another work, Abbott et al. reported that the ionic conductivity of DEL could be increased by decreasing the size of the cation, which will increase the free volume of DEL, resulting in decreased viscosity and increased ionic conductivity. [89] Overall, ionic conductivity depends on donor-to-acceptor ratios and water content in a particular DEL. [90,91] ## Effect of dilution on physicochemical features of DELs It has been noticed that deep eutectic liquids (DELs) absorb water from the air due to their hygroscopic nature, which influences the properties of the solvent. Although water absorption during preparation may work as an impurity, some researchers intentionally add water in DELs to tweak its properties for the desired application. The reports have suggested that adding water to a particular DEL leads to changes in various physicochemical properties, mainly density, melting point, surface tension, viscosity, polarity, and conductivity. Meng et al. [92] evaluated the change in the melting point of DEL containing ChCl and urea by adding water. The solvent's melting point decreased from 30°C to 15°C by adding 5% water. [92] Another group also evaluated the effect of dilution on the physiochemical properties of DEL-based on ChCl and urea. These researchers observed a remarkable decrease of up to 22% in viscosity and a slight reduction of 0.14% in density by adding a 0.008 mass fraction of water. [93] In another report, adding 6% water in ChCl and urea-based DEL increased conductivity by ten times and decreased viscosity by 16 times. [94] Paradiso et al. [95] found that adding water into a DEL comprising glucose and lactic acid decreased the solvent's viscosity to a significant level where it can be used for various extractions. [95] Shah and Mjalli [51] observed that conductivity of ChCl and urea-containing DELs can increase up to three folds for 10% dilution with water which was associated with an 80% decrease in viscosity. A similar kind of behavior was observed for the density, viscosity, and conductivity of various NaDELs. [91] Gabriele et al. [96] studied the impact of water content on conductivity and viscosity of DELs comprising ChCl as HBA and various HBD species and found that viscosity of a particular DEL was almost halved at 10% water content while the conductivity increased by 15 times. The highest value of conductivity was observed for the DELs containing 60% water. Nunes et al. [71] investigated the effect of water content on the surface tension of a DEL composed of octanoic acid and menthol and observed that an increase in water content initially decreased the surface tension, followed by an increase. A similar trend has been also observed for DEL containing malonic acid and ChCl. [97] It can be speculated that water in a particular DEL affects the network of hydrogen bonds and other interactions. It should be further kept in mind that water itself can act as HBD to strengthen the binding forces up to specific water content, after which dilution weakens the overall network's strength. [15,98,99] However, in addition to the alteration of 1644 [icon] M. MUSHTAQ ET AL. properties, the integrity of a DEL system can also be jeopar- dized by the inclusion of water. [100] An increase in the number of bonding network arrangements makes these liquids complex to study and predicted but raises an opportunity of tunable character for end-user applications. The researchers have found that most of the interactions in these liquids are intramolecular bonds between HBA and HBD. At the same time, even complex structures are possible due to the establishment of hydrogen bonds between HBDs and HBAs. During molecular studies, four types of H-bonds have been located whose relative contribution depends upon the mixing ratio of HBD and HBA. In the case of ChCl and alcohols, the HBA possesses a spatial location near HBD. [101] Meanwhile, it has been speculated that deep eutectic liquid keeps its structure for up to 50% water content but thermophysical properties like viscosity, surface tension, and density decrease with the increase in water content. The radial distribution function (RDF) has also been applied to probe the variation in structural features of deep eutectic mixtures with different water contents. The RDF discloses the formation of isosbestic-like points for chloride-water and chloride-urea interactions whose proportion (but not arrangement) increases with the increase in hydration level. [102] In the case of hydrophilic deep eutectic liquids like ChCl/Urea or ChCl/ethylene glycol, the presence of water even below traces may form a quaternary system in which water can act as HBD or HBA depending upon its molecular environment. The experimental and theoretical modulation indicates that water can compete with any of constituting HBD or HBA and disrupt its ratio, thus making the mixture a quaternary system. According to Vilková et al., [102] the absence of isosbestic-like points for chloride-chloride and chloride-choline interactions suggests that two types of structures exist. Several studies have already claimed heterogeneity or the presence of microphases, i.e., water-in-deep eutectic mixture or deep-eutectic mixture-in-water. The change in hydration level mediates transitions between these microphases. In the case of hydrophobic DELs, Kivelä et al. [103] comprehensively studied the structural variation and change in the thermophysical characteristics of a hydrophobic deep eutectic liquid (HDEL) comprising a 1:2 mixture of decanoic acid and tetrabutylammonium chloride. The presence of water even below 2.5% (wt) can significantly affect the physicochemical features of the mixture formed. In particular, the density, viscosity, and melting point of HDEL increase linearly with the increase in water content but the electrical conductivity exhibit a nonlinear dependence because of changes in the charge carriers. The molecular dynamics and simulations study indicate the structural clustering involving hydration on the chloride-carboxylic acid hydrogen bonds. In the absence of water, chloride binds to decanoic acid via hydrogen bond and then forms ion pairing with tetrabutylammonium chloride's strong electrostatic interaction. The intermolecular interaction produces a molecular network in which molecular motions become restricted. The presence of water may break the interaction between chloride and chloride-carboxylic acid and induce the ion pair formation between tetrabutylammonium and chlorides. Water can also hydrate carboxylic acids and chlorides to induce dynamic nanoscale phase segregation. The authors also claim that the composition range for the liquid solvent becomes wide due to the higher hydrogen bonding capacity of chlorides. Rodriguez et al.[104] also noted that water in the combin- ation of ChCl and carboxylic acids could avoid esterification. However, the esterification reaction may accelerate during drying. The authors recommend that ChCl and carboxylic acid type binary mixtures can only be applied once the moisture level or ester formed is adequately quantified. Zhekenov et al.[15] have noted that adding water in a par- ticular DEL improves the interaction between water and HBD, cation of HBA and water, and anion of HBA and water. In the case of ChCl:U and ChCl:Glycerol, the strength of the hydrogen bond between chloride-HBD decreases drastically. Likewise, the addition of water up to 5% (w/w) can get absorbed in the molecular matrix of liquid and does not affect the physicochemical attributes of liquids. However, the further addition of water will dampen the intermolecular and intra-molecular interactions drastically. ## Green features of deep eutectic liquids With the emergence of the green chemistry approach, the exploitation of eco-friendly and benign liquids has become indispensable. For the last couple of decades, deep eutectic liquids (DELs) particularly those composed of natural HBD and HBA species have been considered green and eco-friendly for certain traits. First of all, the intercalation between HBD and HBA species can produce liquids practical nonvolatile, and benign to the environment. The type III and advanced types of DELs comprising tertiary amines, carboxylic acids, and alcohols are often biodegradable with no toxicity, and low reactivity with water makes them an ideal solvent for various analytical applications. Besides, the low- production cost with a great variety of readily available raw materials is the cherry on top. [5,135] The tailorable features of DELs have recently attracted researchers heading toward green chemistry routes. Likewise, the variation in the mobility, density, viscosity, surface tension, and electrical conductance of DELs with the change in nature/mixing ratios of HBD/HBA and moisture level/water content can also work as a new areas of research. The researchers now have adopted theoretical and practical models to explore the effect of water on the physicochemical characteristics of DELs. As many of the DEL formulations contain compounds with low or zero toxicity (including food-grade components like glucose, fructose, and certain amino acids), they have the potential to be evaluated as extraction and synthesis solvents. Many studies have been conducted in this regard to grade the cytotoxic profile of DELs. Haerens et al. [136] reported that DELs comprising ChCl and EG were harmless to the environment compared to most ionic liquids, which possess a certain threat. These authors also found above DELs recyclable from various materials but further studies are required to establish this CRITICAL REVIEWS IN ANALYTICAL CHEMISTRY [icon] 1645 opportunity. [136] Nevertheless, it would not be fair to declare the DELs generally regarded as safe (GRAS) with the avail-able record of clinical data but those containing natural HBD and HBA species like sugars, organic acids, and certain amino acids can be declared nontoxic or eco-friendly as the components are biodegradable and nontoxic. [137,138] Huang et al. [139] prepared thirteen different combinations of NaDELs using ChCl, Glycerol, sugars, amino acids, and claimed that the majority of prepared NaDELs were non-toxic and biodegradable. Likewise, Bajkacz and Adamek[140] claim that NaDELs comprising ChCl: Glucose, Lactic acid: Glucose, and Fructose: Glucose: sucrose lactic acid: glucose, glucose: choline chloride, and fructose: glucose: sucrose are nontoxic and biodegradable. # Recycling of DELs Reusing/Recycling solid catalysts and liquids solvents have been a highly appreciated and desirable approach for sustainability and economic point of view. Nevertheless, it is always difficult to recycle a good solvent for thermodynamic constraints during isolation, enrichment, and/or purification. Needless to say, these steps often become necessary to isolate the solutes/analytes of interest while using DELs as an extraction solvent. There exist a lack of sound knowledge and understanding about energetics and mechanisms to recycle a DEL combination after use, still, many researchers undertaking extraction of plant bioactives from agricultural resources or spent electrode materials from lithium-ion batteries claimed these liquids are re-useable up to four to five cycles. [14,141] Some researchers also observed a decline in the extraction efficiency, performance, and overall composition of the tested DEL System. [142,143] For example, Di Gioia et al., [144] claim no loss of performance for a DEL system comprising ChCl and urea (1:2) after four cycles of application, while Kumar et al. [107] found the NaDELs comprising lactic acid and ChCl (5:1) was effective for lignin extraction till four cycles. Another study says that xylan solubility in the aqueous solution of ChCl and acetic acid-based DEL decreased by 5% after the first two cycles, while DEL constituents could be recycled up to four times. [145] The ways followed for recycling a particular DEL solvent involve evaporation under reduced pressure. [99,146-148] No doubt few researchers checked the purity of recycled DELs by monitoring particular functional groups via FT-IR. [149] However, these methods are only effective to concentrate a DELs system via evaporation of water or other volatiles. The DELs have very low vapor pressure and likewise, the analytes with low vapor cannot be evaporated rotary type evaporators. The pervaporation or reverse osmosis may work as an alternative choice for the recycling of DELs but this technology also fails for higher moisture levels and ionic strength. The magnetic field can also be a good opportunity to recycle DEL after application, this approach has been applied to recover DEL composed of ChCl and tetra-cholorferrate (FeCl4). [150] The recycling of DELs from extraction or reaction media needs more exhaustive and comprehensive studies to derive through a straight-way methodology and right now it would be fair to say that recycling or isolation of deep eutectic liquids after their application is still an un-addressed chal- lenge regarding the utilization of these green liquids as solvents. Applications of deep eutectic liquids (DELs) as extraction solvents The advent of modern chromatography and spectroscopic instruments has revolutionized the resolution and sensitivity of analytical assays. Meanwhile, it has been realized that the results of the chromatographic or spectroscopic analysis can be as good as the sample preparation or extraction step had been. The later theory diverted the whole community of analytical chemists to work on some robust and efficient sample preparation or extraction methods. The use of toxic and volatile organic solvents for the dissolution/extraction/elution/washing of the samples or standards has been extensively criticized from human health and environmental safety point of view. The discovery of DELs has opened new hope in many areas of life and physical sciences, particularly in the under-addressed areas of sample preparation or extraction. During the last couple of decades, the DELs have been extensively investigated for the extraction or purification of analytes of almost all types (organic, inorganic, proteinic, volatile, nonvolatile, etc.). The data plotted in Figure 4a and b manifests the steadily growing trend in the research published on DELs (b) and their use as an extraction solvent (a). The earlier trend of DELs usage for various extraction procedures started with type III DEL consisting of ChCl as HBA paired with glycerol, urea, or ethylene glycol as HBDs. [151] However, with the advent of time, alternative HBDs like amides, alcohols, sugars, amines, carboxylic acid, and HBAs such as imidazolium salts, amino acids, sugars, tetraalkylammonium salts, and carboxylic acids got promoted. [152] Hydrophobic DELs are commonly used as solvent systems in aqueous samples for better phase separation than traditional solvents. [153] It has been noted that the properties of DELs are somewhat different from the individual components. These liquids, unlike the organic solvent, could not be applied in pure, instead, the researchers need to incorporate these liquids with conventional solvents like water, ethanol, or methanol for liquid-liquid extraction (LLE), heat-assisted extraction (HAE), microwave-assisted extraction (MAE), or ultrasound-assisted extraction (UAE) as manifested from the generic layout shown in Figure 5. The nature of co-solvent, types of irradiation (thermal, microwave, or ultrasound), the mechanism of separation (partition or dispersion), and application scale decide the type of extraction technique. This section describes some typical examples regarding the utilization of DELs in different types of extrac- tion methods. **Liquid-liquid extraction (LLE)** The foods derived from different plant species are reported to contain numerous bioactives, which are of prime import-ance due to their potential biological activities. In addition to applying DELs in various fields of life and physical sci-ence, these liquids have been relentlessly applied to extract bioactive compounds from agricultural sources by applying LLE. For example, Đorđević et al. [160] applied ChCl:urea (1:2) and triethanolamine:glycerol (1:2) like DELs, diluted (75/25 v/v) with ethanol and water for the extraction of phenolic compounds from black mustard seed. The authors found that mixing triethanolamine:glycerol-based DEL with ethanol (75/25 v/v) offered higher recovery of phenolics like ellagic, syringic, gallic, and caffeic acids from the powder mustard black seeds. Likewise, Wojeicchowski et al. [161] found that the DEL system comprising ChCl as HBA and 1,2-propanediol as HBD premixed with water (50:50 v/v) when applied at 65°C at a liquid to solid ratio of 40 recov- ered 220% more phenolics. de Almeida Pontes et al. [162] claimed 15% higher recovery rates of phenolics from olive leaves while applying ChCl diluted with water (50:50 v/v) at 54°C and 400 rpm of shaking speed. Liu et al. [163] tested the efficacy of different combinations of DELs for the extraction of tocopherols from soybean oil. The results showed that DEL containing p-cresol and ChCl exhibited the best extrac- tion efficiency for all required isomers. This DEL combin- ation may form strong π-π interaction with tocopherols. Abdul Hadi et al. [109] also evaluated the efficacy of DELs based on ChCl and carboxylic acids for the extraction of tocols (tocopherols and tocotrienols) via liquid-liquid extrac- tion. It was reported that the use of DELs promoted the recovery of tocotrienols and overall yield increased with increasing the amount of DEL (Table 2). Aydin et al. [114] were able to extract and purify curcumin from various food and tea samples via vortex-assisted extraction using DEL containing ChCl and phenol in combination with organic solvent tetrahydrofuran, which acted as an emulsifier. The spectroscopic analysis showed a high concentration of cur- cumin in the extract obtained at pH 4.0 with this DEL combination. [114] Tan et al. [164] used various DEL combinations to extract plant growth regulators from different vegetable oils and found that a DEL made up of ethylene glycol and tetraethy- lammonium chloride offered good extraction efficiency for three plant growth regulators. [164] Qi et al. [165] prepared nine combinations of DEL to extract flavonoids from _Equisetum palustre_. Their results showed that the polar fla- vonoids were extracted with the highest efficiency in DEL based on choline chloride, betaine, and ethylene glycol. Nam et al. [166] tested the efficacy of various DEL combinations for extracting flavonoids from _Flos sophorae_. The best extraction efficiency of quercetin was noted with DEL con- sisting of choline chloride and glucose, while choline chlor- ide and xylose were best for the extraction of kaempferol and isorhamnetin. Tang et al. [167] utilized different DEL combinations to extract Myricetin from _Chamaecyparis_ _obtusa_ and found that the targeted flavonoids were extracted with maximum efficiency in DEL based on choline chloride and 1,4-butanediol. [123] applied ChCl, and PEG (1:2.5) based deep eutectic liquid along with 35% (v/v) of water as an extraction solvent for ultrasound-assisted extraction (UAE) of crocins from (Gardenia jasminoides Ellis). The solvent system comprising DEL of ChCl and PEG was labeled as tailor-made and suitable for affinity-based crocins extraction. The prepared solvent system offered higher surface tension, polarity, and electrical conductivity. However, its extraction efficiency was attributed to the extent of available hydrogen bonds. Liu et al. [113] also evaluated the efficacy of various DEL combinations for efficient extraction of sesamol from sesame oil via ultrasound-assisted liquid-liquid microextraction (UALLME) which was subsequently determined by HPLC-DAD analysis. The authors claim that DEL, composed of ethylene glycol and ChCl offered a better yield regarding the extraction of sesamol. [113] Khezeli et al. [183] also employed the UALLME technique to extract three phenolics (cinnamic acid, ferulic acid, and caffeic acid) from cinnamon, almond, and olive oil using different combinations of DELs. This study's results indicate that DELs are far better in phenolic extraction efficiency than conventional solvents. [183] Garcia et al. [184] extracted different phenolics from olive oil using a DEL system containing ChCl as an HBA paired with various HBDs and the results showed that DEL based on ChCl and xylitol and ChCl paired with 1,2-propanediol showed superior results with remarkable extraction efficiency (30-70%) as compared to methanol and water (conventional solvents). Astonishing higher enrichment factor i.e., 444.59-516.58% of apigenin and luteolin, were observed[29] by applying ChCl:polyethylene glycol (1:8) diluted with 40% H2O. These authors tested thirty four ChCl and betaine-based DEL combinations and found that betaine hydrochloride and propylene glycol form two different types of hydrogen bonds and water molecules play an important role in the interaction between HBD and HBA. Mansur et al. [185] tested the efficacy of eighteen combinations of DELs to extract flavonoids from buckwheat sprouts via UAE. It was observed that DEL containing ChCl and triethylene glycol (1:2) offered a higher extraction yield during UAE. The citrus peel has been ranked as a sustainable source of fiber and flavonoids. Using ultrasonic irradiation, various DEL combinations were prepared to extract flavonoids from citrus peel. The most promising feature of these liquids rises for their tailorable nature i.e., a change in HBD/HBA ratios or moisture level can drastically change the melting point, viscosity, surface tension, and electrical conductance. For a similar reason, a great deal of research has become into practice to test the suitability of these liquids in various fields, including modification and synthesis of sorbents, electrochemistry, chromatography, electrophoresis, and various separation process with a particular focus on the extraction of bioactive compounds. In addition, their biodegradable nature with no toxicity and low reactivity with water makes them an ideal solvent for various analytical applications. Besides, their low-cost production with a great variety of readily available raw materials is the cherry on top.^[5,135] Applying deep-eutectic liquids as an extraction solvent can lead the separation technology into green and sustainable analytical chemistry. However, it may take a couple of exhausting decades as these liquids face many logical and technical challenges. First of all, the formation of DELs needs to be authenti- cated and carefully characterized as it does not involve any chemical reaction rather it happens due to reversible inter- molecular interactions or entanglement between HDB and 1652 [icon: stylized cup] M. MUSHTAQ ET AL. HBA species. Another technical challenge is concerned with the thermal stability of these liquids. The available know- ledge regarding the mechanism, formation, and characteriza- tion of DELs shows that the thermal stability of these liquids, particularly those prepared from natural HBDs and HBAs stands questionable. Overall, mixing a deep eutectic liquid (DEL) with water often increases mobility, decreases viscosity and density, and improves the electrical conductance of the resultant solutions but the final mixtures may behave as binary or ternary solution rather than a deep-eutectic liquid. This may lead to completely astonishing/ambiguous outcomes and there is a prompt need to re-define deep-eutectic liquids. In the case of hydrophobic deep eutectic liquids, the water contamination or moisture tremendously affects the geometry and physicochemical features of the liquid formed. Some studies say that the addition of water up to 5% (w/w) can get absorbed in the molecular matrix of liquid and does not affect the physicochemical attributes of liquids. However, the further addition of water will dampen the intermolecular and intra-molecular interactions drastically. This variation can be further exploited to render these liquids more tailorable. Another key hurdle regarding the use of DELs as extrac- tion solvent raises for the relatively higher viscosities, den- sities, and surface tension of these liquids. In this context, many opportunities are available to design these DEL fea- tures of DELs by changing the stoichiometric ratios of HBDs and HBAs, mixing techniques, and molecular dynam- ics. These opportunities are at least more fascinating and more accessible than those available regarding ionic liquids. The simple but less sustainable way to optimize the physico- chemical features of DELs for their application as extraction solvents involves mixing these liquids with conventional organic solvents or water. For example, Đorđević et al. [160] have observed that mixing of ChCl and Urea (1:2) or Triethanolamine and glycerol (1:2) based solvent with water or ethanol offered a higher extraction yield of phenolic com- pounds from black mustard seed. In another study, Wojeicchowski et al. [161] report that mixing ChCl and 1,2- propanediol-based DEL system with water (50:50 v/v) lowers its density and viscosity and improves the solubility of rose- mary phenolics. Meanwhile, the molecular modeling data (COSMO-RS) prediction indicates that the addition of water to the above DEL system does not improve the solubility of analytes, which implies that dilution of that particular DEL with water has improved the mass-transfer rates not the sol- ubilities. These trends need more comprehensive trials before reaching final conclusion. The recycling/recovery of DEL system from the analytes/ extracts exist as an unaddressed challenge. Many researchers claim that DELs especially NaDELs are recyclable but these claims lack sound technical and practical background. The dispersive type (DLLME) and salting-out assisted microex- traction need to be further investigated for the intelligent recycling of DELs from the matrix. A magnetic recycling method has been reported to recycle ChCl and FeCl4 based DEL systems from heptanal and hexanal extracted from edible oils.[150] ## Conclusions The search for novel green solvents has been the talk of the town since the mid of 20th century. Deep-eutectic liquids (DELs) have emerged as potential solvents for their characteristic and tunable features. Besides, the involvement of inexpensive and readily available HBDs and HBAs and easily scaleable development protocols, these liquids stand among the most studied materials in 21st century. The natural deep-eutectic liquids (NaDELs) for their biocompatibility and low toxicity are more potential candidates to serve as a sustainable alternative to conventional toxic solvents. In addition, the nonvolatile character of DEL allows them to be paired with analytical instruments like UV-Visible spectrophotometer and HPLC for further analysis. However, this very nonvolatile property of DEL offers an isolation challenge at the end of extraction or synthesis. To put the whole discussion in a nutshell, it can be said that the future of DEL is quite auspicious as it has the potential to serve as a sustainable alternative for novel appli- cations. However, to utilize DEL to its fullest potential, more coherent and systematic research need to be dedicated to intermolecular entanglement, radial distribution function, target-oriented molecular modeling, solvatochromic poten- tial, recyclability, and designable physicochemical attributes of DEL systems. The recycling of DELs from extraction or reaction media needs more exhaustive and comprehensive studies to derive through a straight-way methodology and right now it would be fair to say that recycling or isolation of deep eutectic liquids after their application is still an un- addressed challenge regarding the utilization of these green liquids as solvents.
